p64.title: Print “سلام” five times
p64.statement:
Print the word **سلام** (the Persian word for “hello”) **five times**; each time on its own line.

This problem has no input.
hints: `range(5)` gives five repeats.
If you do not use the counter, you can name it `_`.
p64.guideTitle: Print “سلام” five times — repeating with for and while
mistakes: Writing `print` five times separately: it works, but a loop is made for repeating the same job.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range(5)
steps: This problem has no input; only a repeating loop is needed.
With `range(5)` we run the loop five times.
In each round we print the word `سلام`.
explain: `range(5)` gives the five numbers zero to four, so the body of the loop runs five times. The variable `i` is not used in this problem, but `for` needs a variable.
Each `print` writes a new line; so `سلام` appears five times, each time on its own line.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with a counter
steps: We start the counter from zero.
As long as the counter is less than five, we print `سلام`.
In each round we increase the counter by one.
explain: The condition `i < 5` becomes false after five rounds. If we do not increase the counter, the loop becomes endless and the program never ends.
Both methods have the same output. `for` is shorter when we know the number of repeats in advance, and `while` is more suitable when we control the condition ourselves.

p65.title: Squares of the numbers 1 to n
p65.statement:
Read a natural number `n` (`n ≥ 1`).

Print the squares of the numbers `1` to `n`, **each on its own line**. For example, for `n = 4` the output is 1, 4, 9 and 16.
hints: The square of a number is the number times itself.
Run the loop from 1 to `n`; so set the end of `range` to `n + 1`.
p65.guideTitle: Squares of the numbers 1 to n — input and calculating in a loop
mistakes: Starting from zero: the square of zero is printed and the number 1 is not the first output.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range(1, n + 1)
steps: We read the number `n` from the input.
With `range(1, n + 1)` we go over the numbers 1 to n.
We calculate and print the square of each number with `i * i`.
explain: The square of a number means multiplying it by itself, so `i * i`. For `n = 4` we have 1, 4, 9 and 16, which are the squares of 1, 2, 3 and 4.
The end of the range is `n + 1` so that `n` itself is included. This is the same point that must be checked in all ranges.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with a counter
steps: We read the number `n`.
We start the counter from one and continue as long as it has not gone above `n`.
In each round we print the square of the counter and then increase the counter by one.
explain: This method builds the same squares with a `while` loop. The condition `i <= n` includes `n` itself, so the last square, `n × n`, is printed.
If `n` is read from the user, the program works for every natural value of `n`.

p66.title: Countdown with while from 5 to 1
p66.statement:
Using a **while** loop (and no for), count backwards from **5** to **1** and print each number **on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Start a variable with 5 and continue as long as it is greater than or equal to 1.
After each print, subtract one from the variable.
mistakes: Forgetting to subtract from the counter: the loop becomes endless.

solutions.name: Method 1: a decreasing counter i
steps: We start the counter from 5.
As long as the counter is greater than or equal to one, we print it.
In each round we subtract one from the counter.
explain: In a countdown the counter decreases in each round. The condition `i >= 1` keeps the number 1, so the last output is 1.
This problem accepts only `while`; so we must write a loop with a condition that controls the counter ourselves.

solutions.name: Method 2: a variable n and decreasing it
steps: We set a variable named `n` equal to 5.
As long as `n` is positive, we print it.
After each print, we subtract one from `n`.
explain: This method does the same counting with another variable name. The condition `n > 0` is equivalent to `n >= 1`, because all the values are integers.
Choosing the variable name matters: `n` is expressive for a number that goes from top to bottom.

p67.title: Counting up with while from 20 to 25
p67.statement:
Using a **while** loop (and no for), print the numbers **20 to 25**, **each on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Start the counter with 20 and continue as long as it is less than or equal to 25.
After each print, increase the counter by one.
p67.guideTitle: Counting up with while from 20 to 25
mistakes: The condition `i < 25` instead of `i <= 25`: the number 25 is not printed.

solutions.name: Method 1: an increasing counter i
steps: We start the counter from 20.
As long as the counter has not gone above 25, we print it.
In each round we increase the counter by one.
explain: The condition `i <= 25` includes the number 25. The two boundaries of this problem are 20 and 25, and both are seen in the output.
This problem accepts only `while`, so we must increase the counter ourselves in the loop.

solutions.name: Method 2: a variable n from 20 to 25
steps: We set the variable `n` equal to 20.
As long as `n` is less than or equal to 25, we print it.
After each print, we increase `n` by one.
explain: This method writes the same counting with another name. The structure of the loop is fixed: start, condition, print and update.
Both methods have exactly the same output; the difference is in the variable name, and this difference is not important for the rest of the course.

p68.title: Even numbers from 0 to 10 with while
p68.statement:
Using a **while** loop (and no for), print the even numbers **0, 2, 4, …, 10**, **each on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Start the counter from 0 and increase it by two each time.
Write the continuing condition so that 10 is printed too.
p68.guideTitle: Even numbers from 0 to 10 with while
mistakes: Increasing the counter by 1: the odd numbers are printed too.

solutions.name: Method 1: a step of two
steps: We start the counter from zero.
As long as it has not gone above 10, we print it.
In each round we add two.
explain: Starting from zero and adding 2 always gives even numbers. The condition `i <= 10` includes 10 itself.
This problem accepts only `while`; the step of two in this loop takes the place of `range` with a step.

solutions.name: Method 2: halving a counter
steps: We start the variable `k` from zero; it is half of the even number.
As long as twice `k` has not gone above 10, we print the number twice `k`.
In each round we increase `k` by one.
explain: This method builds the even numbers from their halves: 0, 1, 2 … 5, and doubles each one. It is a different method that shows any arithmetic pattern can be built with a counter.
The condition `k * 2 <= 10` keeps the boundary 10 as it should be.

p69.title: Countdown with step 5 to zero
p69.statement:
Using a **while** loop (and no for), count backwards from **50** to **0** with a step of **5**. Print each number **on its own line**: 50, 45, 40, …, 5, 0.

This problem has no input.
hints: Start the counter with 50 and subtract five each time.
The continuing condition must include the number zero too.
mistakes: The condition `i > 0`: the number zero is not printed.

solutions.name: Method 1: subtracting five
steps: We start the counter from 50.
As long as the counter is greater than or equal to zero, we print it.
In each round we subtract five.
explain: By subtracting 5 in each round, the counter goes from 50 to 45, 40 and so on down to 0. The condition `i >= 0` prints zero too.
The important point is that the step 5 must be exactly in the body of the loop; if we forget it, the loop becomes endless.

solutions.name: Method 2: a variable n with step 5
steps: We set the variable `n` equal to 50.
As long as `n` is non-negative, we print it.
After each print, we subtract five from `n`.
explain: This method shows the same pattern with another name. "Non-negative" means zero or positive, and this is exactly the condition that includes the number zero.
If we had set the condition to `n > 0`, zero would not be printed and the test would reject it.

p70.title: Powers of 2 up to 64
p70.statement:
Using a **while** loop (and no for), print the numbers **1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64**, **each on its own line**. Each number is double the previous one.

This problem has no input.
hints: Start from 1 and multiply the number by 2 each time.
When the number becomes greater than 64, the loop must end.
p70.guideTitle: Powers of 2 up to 64 — multiplying by two with while
mistakes: Using addition `x + 2` instead of multiplication: the numbers do not become powers of 2.

solutions.name: Method 1: doubling the number
steps: We start the number from 1.
As long as it has not gone above 64, we print it.
In each round we double the number.
explain: Each power is double the previous one: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64. Multiplying by 2 builds this pattern, and the condition `i <= 64` keeps the last number.
This problem is solved with `while`, because the number of rounds is not known in advance; the loop continues until the number passes the limit.

solutions.name: Method 2: a power variable and multiplying by two
steps: We set the variable `power` equal to 1.
As long as `power` has not become greater than 64, we print it.
In each round we replace `power` with `power * 2`.
explain: This method writes the same pattern with the variable name `power`. A meaningful name makes the program easy to understand.
If we want to print larger numbers, we only change the boundary 64; the logic of the program stays the same.

p71.title: Sum of 1 to n with while
p71.statement:
Read a natural number `n` (`n ≥ 1`).

Using a **while** loop (no for and no sum), print the total of the numbers `1` to `n`. For example, for `n = 4` the answer is 10.
hints: Make a variable for the total (from zero) and a counter (from 1).
In each repeat, add the counter to the total and then increase the counter by one.
p71.guideTitle: Total of 1 to n with while
mistakes: Forgetting to increase the counter: the loop does not end.

solutions.name: Method 1: a counter from 1 towards n
steps: We read the number `n` and start the total from zero and the counter from 1.
As long as the counter has not gone above `n`, we add it to the total and increase the counter by one.
At the end we print the total.
explain: This method builds the sum `1 + 2 + … + n` step by step. In each repeat one number is added to the total.

solutions.name: Method 2: a counter from n towards 1
steps: We read the number `n` and start the counter with `n`.
As long as the counter is positive, we add it to the total and subtract one from it.
explain: Adding the numbers in reverse order gives the same result. This method only starts from the other side.

p91.title: Sum of the numbers in a list
p91.statement:
Write a function named `list_sum(nums)` that returns the sum of all the numbers in the list `nums`. If the list is empty, the answer is `0`.

This problem is a **function test**.
hints: Make a variable from zero and add the numbers to it in a loop.
If the list is empty, the loop does not run and the sum is that zero.
p91.guideTitle: Sum of the numbers in a list — a function and going over
mistakes: Starting the sum from the first number with `total = nums[0]`: an empty list gives an error.

solutions.name: Method 1: adding in a variable with for
steps: We set a variable `total` equal to zero.
With `for` we take each number of the list and add it to `total`.
At the end we return `total`; if the list is empty, zero is returned.
explain: This function takes a list as input and returns the sum. The variable `total` starts from zero, so for an empty list zero is returned, and that is the correct result.
`return` takes the place of `print`: the function gives the value back to the program that called it so that the test can check it.

solutions.name: Method 2: going over with an index and while
steps: We start the sum from zero and the index from zero too.
As long as the index is smaller than the length of the list, we add the number at that place to the sum.
We move the index forward by one in each round and at the end we return the sum.
explain: `nums[i]` is the number at place `i` in the list. `len(nums)` gives the length of the list, so the loop goes over exactly all the members. If the list is empty, the loop does not run and `total` stays zero.
This method builds the same sum with an indexed pass; `for` and this method are both correct, but here we practise the indexing too.

p92.title: List of squares
p92.statement:
Read the natural number `n` (`n ≥ 1`).

Print the list of the squares of the numbers `1` to `n` **in the form of a Python list**, with `print` on the list itself. For example, for `n = 3` the output is `[1, 4, 9]`.
hints: Make an empty list and in a loop add the squares to it with `append`.
At the end print the list itself with `print`, not its members.
mistakes: Printing each square separately: the output must be a list.

solutions.name: Method 1: append in a loop
steps: We read the number `n` and make an empty list.
With `for` we go from 1 to `n` and `append` the square of each number.
We print the list.
explain: `append` adds the new member to the end of the list. After the loop, the list has all the squares and `print` shows it in the form of a list.

solutions.name: Method 2: a counter from zero to n-1
steps: We make the empty list.
We run the loop `n` times and in each one add the square of `i + 1`.
explain: The counter starts from zero, so for the numbers 1 to `n` we must take `i + 1`. The result is the same list.
